lines: \begin{abstract}

-Modular LLM agents that route between neural reasoning and deterministic computation promise improved reliability, yet understanding \emph{what} drives the value of routing decisions remains unclear. We introduce a formal diagnostic framework---episode-level counterfactual analysis with the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF) metric---that decomposes routing signal into death-avoidance and non-death components by running complete episodes under pure strategies and comparing final outcomes. The framework requires only paired episode outcomes under two modalities with binary success/failure indicators. We demonstrate this in environments with catastrophic failure modes. Applied to ScienceWorld (11 of 30 task types, 245 episodes, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels} (75 of 95, penalty-independent) are driven by death asymmetry; under ScienceWorld's actual penalty ($P{=}100$), this corresponds to DAF $= 90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$, score-level, $P$-dependent). Per-task death rate correlates with routing signal ($r{=}0.97$), though this is largely a mathematical consequence of death dominance (partial $r{=}0.02$, $p{=}0.91$ after controlling for $\delta \cdot P$; \S\ref{sec:death-decomp}). An exploratory router yields an informative negative: episode-level balanced accuracy remains at or below chance at practical scales (0.6B--1.7B) and reaches only $59.0\%$ at 4B ($p < 0.005$), a disproportionate cost for $+9$\,pp above random---consistent with the analytical framework being more efficient than brute-force learned routing. Cross-environment analysis on MATH ($N{=}300$) shows the death-driven routing signal is not statistically detectable without a death penalty ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$). A Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct replication (7 task types, 70 episodes) confirms direction-consistent death patterns for all task types ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ death-rate differential). These findings indicate that in environments with catastrophic failure modes, routing value is dominated by safety---the routing problem reduces to safety-first modality selection rather than efficiency optimization.

\section{Introduction}

Large language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.
A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}

Existing routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.
Toolformer \cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.
More recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \cite{mtrouter-2026}.
The shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.
But this assumption has never been systematically verified: \emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}

We propose a \emph{formal diagnostic framework} for answering this question. The framework comprises (i)~episode-level counterfactual labeling under pure strategies (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:labeling}), and (ii)~the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF), a metric that decomposes the routing score gap into death-avoidance and non-death components (\S\ref{sec:daf}). Applied to ScienceWorld, the framework reveals a surprisingly concentrated answer: \textbf{78.9\% of non-tie routing labels arise from death asymmetry} (75 of 95, penalty-independent); under ScienceWorld's default penalty ($P{=}100$), this corresponds to DAF $= 90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$).
The internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.
Once death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$.

This framework addresses a methodological gap.
The standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.
In ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\S\ref{sec:collection}).
Keyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\S\ref{sec:baselines}).
Our counterfactual approach runs complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compares episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\S\ref{sec:collection}). The framework is applicable to any environment with controllable modality comparison and binary catastrophic outcomes, requiring only paired episode outcomes under two modalities.

Our prescreening selected task types showing \emph{any} modality difference (not death-specific); the finding that 19 of 30 task types show no routing signal itself confirms signal sparsity. Among the 11 selected types (245 episode pairs), the full deterministic advantage is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points.
Excluding death episodes, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$; 78.9\% of non-tie labels (75 of 95) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent measure.
The penalty-sensitive Death Avoidance Factor (DAF; \S\ref{sec:daf}) is $90.4\%$ (95\% CI: $[81.6\%, 98.8\%]$) at the default penalty $P{=}100$, ranging from 50\% ($P{=}10$) to 98\% ($P{=}500$).
The per-task correlation between death-rate differential and performance gap is $r = 0.97$ ($p < 10^{-6}$, $n = 11$), though this is largely a mathematical consequence of death dominance (partial $r = 0.02$, $p = 0.91$ after controlling for $\delta \cdot P$); we retain it as an internal consistency check (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}).

Two cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.
First, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation (300 problems), using a code interpreter as the deterministic modality, shows a directional trend consistent with the absence of death-driven routing signal: internal reasoning outperforms code interpreter by $+4.3$~pp ($p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$)---the opposite direction from ScienceWorld.
In the absence of death risk, the deterministic advantage is not statistically detectable ($p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$).
Second, a cross-model replication with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (7 task types, 70 episode pairs) shows direction-consistent death patterns for all task types, with a larger death-rate differential ($+34.3\%$ vs.\ $+26.6\%$ for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model}), confirming the phenomenon generalizes across model families.
An exploratory step-level router (Qwen3-1.7B with LoRA) trained on these counterfactual labels achieves $54.1 \pm 5.4\%$ step-level balanced accuracy but only $47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ on held-out episodes---below the always-deterministic baseline---a capacity-dependent limitation confirmed by data scaling ($32{\times}$) ablations; the 4B scale yields $59.0\%$ but the cost is disproportionate to the routing benefit (\S\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{A formal diagnostic framework for routing signal decomposition.}
    We formalize episode-level counterfactual labeling (Algorithm~\ref{alg:labeling}) with the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF) metric, providing a general methodology applicable to environments with controllable modality comparison for quantifying what fraction of routing signal derives from catastrophic-failure avoidance versus non-death performance differences (\S\ref{sec:collection}--\ref{sec:daf}).

    \item \textbf{Death avoidance dominance.}
    On ScienceWorld, 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels stem from death asymmetry (label-level, penalty-independent). The score-level DAF metric reaches $90.4\%$ at $P{=}100$ ($P$-dependent) but varies substantially across penalty settings. An exploratory router trained on these labels fails to outperform the trivial always-deterministic baseline on held-out episodes ($47.1 \pm 2.2\%$ vs.\ $50.0\%$); data scaling ablations confirm this capacity-dependent limitation; scaling to 4B yields $59.0\%$ episode-level accuracy but the cost (4B parameters for $+9$\,pp above random) is disproportionate when DAF $= 90.4\%$ and always-deterministic is trivially near-optimal (\S\ref{sec:death-decomp}--\ref{sec:router-diagnostic}).

    \item \textbf{Cross-context applicability.}
    On MATH ($N{=}300$), where no death penalty exists, internal reasoning directionally outperforms code interpretation ($+4.3$~pp, $p = 0.079$, not reaching $\alpha{=}0.05$), consistent with the framework's prediction that death-avoidance signal should be absent without catastrophic failure. On ALFWorld ($N{=}135$), the framework identifies a qualitatively different mechanism: information asymmetry (access to admissible actions) rather than death avoidance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). True quantitative replication requires a second environment with catastrophic failure (e.g., NetHack, Crafter).
\end{enumerate}
